name: Data Governance Act
evidence_rating: thin: Commission forecasts, registers and enforcement records, two critical legal analyses; no evaluation or causal evidence
summary: The Data Governance Act (applying since September 2023) created a regime for trusted data intermediaries and data altruism. The Commission forecast EUR 7-11 billion for the data economy by 2028, but uptake has been modest - 38 registered intermediaries and 7 altruism organisations by mid-2026 - and many countries were late in setting up authorities. Legal scholars argued the rules could make intermediaries unviable, and in November 2025 the Commission proposed folding the DGA into the Data Act and making the intermediary regime voluntary.

indicators.objective: The proposal has no LFS indicator section; the memorandum promised monitoring via stakeholder surveys, the Support Centre for Data Sharing, records of the European Data Innovation Board and an evaluation study

indicators.indicator: Direct impact on the EU data economy of EUR 7.2-10.9bn in 2028
indicators.evidence: Not measured. The Commission's implementation study (announced with the Digital Omnibus) was not yet published; the Omnibus proposes repealing the DGA and moving its rules into the Data Act.

indicators.indicator: Uptake of notified data intermediation services
indicators.evidence: Measured (activity): the EU register lists 38 data intermediation services notified in 10 Member States (page updated August 2026), concentrated in France (12) and the Netherlands (11). The Commission itself calls the market 'emerging' and proposes making the regime voluntary.
indicators.sources: Commission register of data intermediation services; COM(2025) 837

indicators.evidence: Measured (activity): 7 recognised organisations in 4 Member States (register updated July 2026).
indicators.sources: Commission register of data altruism organisations

indicators.indicator: National competent authorities designated and empowered
indicators.evidence: Slow: letters of formal notice to 18 Member States (May 2024) and reasoned opinions to 10 (December 2024) for failing to designate or empower DGA authorities.

indicators.indicator: Efficiency savings from re-use of protected public-sector data of about EUR 684m a year

literature.citation: European Commission (2020), Impact assessment report accompanying the Data Governance Act proposal (executive summary SWD(2020) 296), SWD(2020) 295
literature.title: Impact assessment report accompanying the Data Governance Act proposal (executive summary SWD(2020) 296)
literature.outcomes: data economy value; compliance costs; public-sector savings
literature.headline: Preferred package worth EUR 7.2-10.9bn to the EU data economy in 2028; labelling cost EUR 20,000-50,000 per intermediary; public-sector set-up EUR 10.6m per Member State with efficiency savings of about EUR 684m a year
literature.summary_plain: The Commission expected the DGA to add EUR 7-11 billion to the EU data economy by 2028 by building trust in data sharing.

literature.citation: von Ditfurth & Lienemann (2022), The Data Governance Act: Promoting or Restricting Data Intermediaries?, Competition and Regulation in Network Industries 23(4)
literature.title: The Data Governance Act: Promoting or Restricting Data Intermediaries?
literature.venue: Competition and Regulation in Network Industries 23(4)
literature.headline: Examines the DGA's prior-notification regime and conditions on data intermediaries (Art. 10-15) and asks whether they promote or restrict trustworthy, competitive data sharing; highlights risks that the conditions restrict intermediaries' business models
literature.summary_plain: Researchers warn that the DGA's strict conditions on data intermediaries may hold back the very services it aims to encourage.

literature.citation: Carovano & Finck (2023), Regulating data intermediaries: The impact of the Data Governance Act on the EU's data economy, Computer Law & Security Review 50: 105830
literature.title: Regulating data intermediaries: The impact of the Data Governance Act on the EU's data economy
literature.headline: DGA rests on questionable assumptions, imposes requirements not all intermediaries can meet and entrenches a form of intermediation that may be economically non-viable; inconsistencies with GDPR, Data Act and DMA; may hinder its own objectives
literature.summary_plain: Legal scholars argue the DGA's design could make data intermediaries commercially unviable and clashes with other EU data laws.

literature.citation: European Commission (2024), Commission calls on 10 Member States to comply with the Data Governance Act, Press release, 16 December 2024
literature.title: Commission calls on 10 Member States to comply with the Data Governance Act
literature.headline: Reasoned opinions to Czechia, Germany, Estonia, Greece, Cyprus, Luxembourg, Austria, Poland, Portugal and Slovenia for not designating or empowering DGA authorities, following letters of formal notice in 2024
literature.summary_plain: Over a year after the DGA applied, ten countries still had not set up the authorities needed to run it.

literature.citation: European Commission (2026), EU registers of data intermediation services and of recognised data altruism organisations, Shaping Europe's digital future (pages updated July-August 2026)
literature.title: EU registers of data intermediation services and of recognised data altruism organisations
literature.venue: Shaping Europe's digital future (pages updated July-August 2026)
literature.headline: 38 data intermediation services notified in 10 Member States; 7 recognised data altruism organisations in 4 Member States
literature.summary_plain: Nearly three years after the DGA applied, 38 data intermediaries and 7 data altruism organisations had registered EU-wide.
literature.quality: count only; no data on volumes shared

literature.citation: European Commission (2025), Proposal for a Digital Omnibus Regulation (repealing Regulation (EU) 2022/868), COM(2025) 837
literature.title: Proposal for a Digital Omnibus Regulation (repealing Regulation (EU) 2022/868)
literature.headline: Proposes repealing the DGA and moving streamlined rules on data intermediation and data altruism into the Data Act; mandatory notification for intermediaries becomes a voluntary label 'for this market to grow'; reporting duties for altruism organisations dropped
literature.summary_plain: In November 2025 the Commission proposed scrapping the DGA as a separate law and making its intermediary rules voluntary, implicitly acknowledging weak uptake.

literature.authors: Gardner, H., Enzerink, S., Page, M., Brincat, A. (Capgemini); Tenge, E., Velcsov, T., Macchioni, M.S. (Spark Legal and Policy Consulting); Lechardoy, L., Spolverato, G. (Open Evidence)
literature.title: Study supporting the evaluation of the Free Flow of Non-Personal Data Regulation, Open Data Directive and Data Governance Act - Final Report
literature.venue: European Commission, DG CONNECT (Publications Office, published 12 January 2026)
literature.method: ex-post evaluation: register analysis of notified data intermediation providers and data altruism organisations, surveys of national competent authorities, interviews with 9 providers, stakeholder surveys and focus groups, legal analysis
literature.outcomes: uptake of data intermediation and data altruism; national implementation; burdens
literature.headline: The DGA is at a 'nascent stage': by October/November 2025 only 27 data intermediation providers had registered in seven Member States (vs 100-150 expected; none in about three quarters of Member States) and only three recognised data altruism organisations existed.
literature.summary_plain: The Commission's contracted evaluation finds that very few businesses or non-profits have signed up to the new trusted data-sharing schemes the act created. Delayed national implementation and unclear benefits of registering hold uptake back.
literature.quality: Official ex-post evaluation; descriptive counts and stakeholder evidence, no counterfactual; small provider sample
literature.interested_party: Commissioned and steered by the Commission (evaluating its own act)
